ch06.f.d.mode: Increase a horizontal pull steadily, or tilt the board steadily
ch06.f.d.mat: Materials of block and surface: they set the static coefficient $\mu_s$ and the kinetic coefficient $\mu_k$
ch06.f.goal.static: Static friction: only as large as needed, at most $\mu_s N$
ch06.f.goal.kinetic: When the block starts to slide, friction drops to $\mu_k N$ ($\mu_k < \mu_s$) and stays there
ch06.f.obs.match: At rest: the $f$ curve lies on the pull $F$ (dashed), $f_s = F$
ch06.f.obs.drop: When $f$ reaches $\mu_s N$ the block starts to slide, $f$ drops to $\mu_k N$ and $v$ starts to grow
ch06.f.obs.angle: Tilting board: sliding starts at the angle with $\tan\theta_c = \mu_s$ (wood 26.6°, ice 5.7°), whatever the mass
ch06.f.obs.mat: On the incline $N = mg\cos\theta$, so $\mu_s N$ shrinks as the angle grows
ch06.f.assume: Block mass 2 kg, the pull grows at 4 N/s, the board tilts at 6°/s and is held at the angle where sliding starts, typical friction coefficients
ch06.c.d.preset: Four situations in which different real forces keep the object on the circle
ch06.c.d.cut: The string breaks after a quarter turn
ch06.c.d.ice: Road friction vanishes after a quarter turn
ch06.c.goal.net: Uniform circular motion: the net force points to the centre and has size $mv^2/r$
ch06.c.goal.notnew: Centripetal force = the radial component of the net force. It is not a new kind of force; tension, friction or a normal force plays that role
ch06.c.obs.string: Ball on a string: the tension $T$ is the centripetal force; gravity and the normal force cancel
ch06.c.obs.flat: Flat curve: static friction $f_s$ is the centripetal force
ch06.c.obs.tilt: Banked curve and conical pendulum: the horizontal component of the tilted force ($N\sin\theta$, $T\sin\theta$) is the centripetal force; the vertical component balances $mg$
ch06.c.obs.cut: Cut string or icy road: once the inward force is gone the object moves straight along the tangent; without an inward net force there is no circular motion. The cut conical pendulum also falls under gravity alone (side view; its tangential motion is perpendicular to the view)
ch06.c.goal.rot: In the frame rotating with the object (a non-inertial frame) the object is at rest: the real forces and the centrifugal force $m\omega^2 r$ add to zero
ch06.c.obs.rot: Rotating frame (bottom): the object stays put while the ground marks turn the other way (clockwise). The inward real force and the outward centrifugal force $F_\text{cf} = m\omega^2 r = mv^2/r$ (dashed) cancel. Centrifugal and Coriolis forces are fictitious forces: no other object exerts them; they are added so that Newton's second law keeps its form in a non-inertial frame
ch06.c.obs.cor: Cut string or icy road, rotating frame: the object moves outward along a path that bends against the rotation. The centrifugal force $m\omega^2 r$ (growing with the distance from the axis) and the Coriolis force $-2m\vec\omega\times\vec v'$ (perpendicular to $\vec v'$) produce that acceleration. In the inertial frame the same motion is a straight line with no horizontal force
ch06.c.assume: Ball on a string: 0.5 kg, radius 1 m, 3 m/s, frictionless table. Curves: 1000 kg, radius 20 m, flat curve at 10 m/s, banked curve at 20° at its design speed (no friction). Conical pendulum: 1 m string at 30°. The top views share one drawn radius; top-view force arrows are scaled relative to $mv^2/r$, side-view force arrows relative to $mg$. Rotating frame: it coincides with the inertial frame at $t = 0$ and turns at $\omega = v/r$. The side view shows only the centrifugal force, which is radial; the Coriolis force, whose direction turns in the horizontal plane, is shown in the top view only
